proof_method_executed: A 5-gate structural audit over the submitted tree (the flush expression inside the kv module, the signal actually connected to the module's flush port together with every producer term of that signal, the fields and write-enables of the SoC-facing fatal error register, the KeyVault error observability paths available to software, and the in-tree specification statements on fatal errors and on hardware clearing of the KeyVault), plus a directed single-DUT simulation of src/keyvault/rtl/kv.sv (13 asserted controls, 0 failures, 1 measured probe) establishing that the flush is a working containment mechanism. Gates evaluated: 5 of 5. The gate that decides proposition A is gate 2, returning kv_flush_signal_fatal_error_terms=1. The gate that decides proposition B is gate 5, returning spec_statements_requiring_keyvault_errors_reported_fatal=0, together with gate 4's engine_register_blocks_with_keyvault_error_status=4.
result_summary:
The candidate makes two separable claims. The first is wrong on the facts. The second is factually correct but is a design scope statement rather than a defect.

Proposition A, that the KeyVault flush responds only to a debug or scan mode transition and therefore does not fire when a fatal error is latched, is refuted by tracing the signal instead of the port name. The expression at src/keyvault/rtl/kv.sv:122-123 does read debugUnlock_or_scan_mode_switch, and that name is what the claim rests on. But a port name is not a contract. At the kv instantiation the port is connected to debug_lock_or_scan_mode_switch (src/integration/rtl/caliptra_top.sv:1208), and that signal is driven at src/integration/rtl/caliptra_top.sv:770 by four terms: debug_lock_switch, scan_mode_switch, device_lifecycle_switch, and cptra_error_fatal. A fatal error already reaches the KeyVault flush (kv_flush_signal_fatal_error_terms=1). cptra_error_fatal is the top-level output the SoC sees (cptra_error_fatal_is_top_level_output=1), not an internal alias, so the term is the real condition and not a lookalike. The term detector carries a contrast check against cptra_in_debug_scan_mode, a signal in the same file that is not fatal-derived and is correctly reported as carrying no fatal term (contrast_signal_fatal_error_terms=0), so the positive reading is discrimination rather than a pattern that matches anything. The module-internal expression is only half of the delivered logic, and reading it alone is what produced the claim.

That the flush is worth reaching was established by measurement rather than assumed. In simulation, a pulse on the flush input overwrites an unlocked entry with the selected debug value 0xaaaaaaaa (CONTROL_C), and it also writes that same debug value into an entry whose lock_wr is set and remains set (CONTROL_D), so the flush is not stoppable by the per-entry lock bits. The write-locked entry is what makes this conclusive: lock_wr does not suppress the read mux (src/keyvault/rtl/kv.sv:234 qualifies reads with lock_use alone), so the debug value is directly observable through the client, whereas a lock_use entry can only be shown to have stopped returning its key material. src/keyvault/rtl/kv.sv:211 is the mechanism, admitting debugUnlock_or_scan_mode_switch as an alternative to the ~lock_wr_q & ~lock_use_q qualifier. checks_run=13 checks_failed=0.

Proposition B, that no KeyVault error condition is reported as a Caliptra fatal error, is factually accurate: CPTRA_HW_ERROR_FATAL declares exactly four error fields, iccm_ecc_unc, dccm_ecc_unc, nmi_pin and crypto_err (src/soc_ifc/rtl/soc_ifc_external_reg.rdl:27-31), with the matching four write-enables at src/soc_ifc/rtl/soc_ifc_top.sv:1378-1381 and no KeyVault term among them. It is not a defect, for two reasons. No in-tree statement requires it (spec_statements_requiring_keyvault_errors_reported_fatal=0); the only in-tree requirement on fatal errors is the recovery rule at docs/CaliptraIntegrationSpecification.md:949, that the SoC shall only recover Caliptra fatal errors via a power-good reset, which says nothing about what must be classified as one. And KeyVault errors are reported, by a different and per-engine path: src/keyvault/rtl/kv_def.rdl:25-36 defines a KV_READ_FAIL and KV_WRITE_FAIL enumeration on an 8-bit ERROR status field, the read and write clients drive it at src/keyvault/rtl/kv_read_client.sv:119 and src/keyvault/rtl/kv_write_client.sv, and four engine register blocks expose it to software (engine_register_blocks_with_keyvault_error_status=4: AES, ECC, HMAC and SHA512). A KeyVault access failure is attributable to the engine that suffered it, which a single global fatal bit could not express. Also relevant to scope: soc_ifc_top has two KeyVault ports, kv_read and kv_rd_resp, and neither is an error input (soc_ifc_keyvault_error_ports=0), so there is no port that exists and goes unused, which would have been a routing gap worth reporting.

Two further measurements are recorded separately and deliberately not merged into either proposition; they are set out under non_findings.

impact: No security impact from proposition A. The opposite of the claim holds: a Caliptra fatal error does destroy KeyVault secrets, because the signal connected to the module's flush port carries cptra_error_fatal as one of its four producer terms, and the flush was measured writing the debug value into every entry including one with a set write lock.

No security impact from proposition B. The absence of a KeyVault field in CPTRA_HW_ERROR_FATAL is a classification scope decision, not a lost report. KeyVault read and write failures reach software through the per-engine KV status ERROR field in four engine register blocks, at a finer granularity than a global fatal bit would provide, and no in-tree statement requires them to be fatal.

Recorded for a future reviewer rather than claimed as a finding: kv_error_intr and kv_notif_intr are tied to zero with a TODO comment at src/integration/rtl/caliptra_top.sv:473-474, so the KeyVault's dedicated interrupt vectors carry nothing. This is a separate observability path from the SoC-facing fatal register and is reported on its own terms; see non_findings.
security_impact_assessment.bypassed_feature: None. A fatal error already triggers the KeyVault flush, and no in-tree requirement assigns KeyVault error conditions to the fatal error register.
attacker_model: An attacker who induces a Caliptra fatal error was assumed, on the claim that KeyVault secrets would survive it. They do not: the fatal error reaches the flush and the flush overwrites every entry with the debug value, bypassing the per-entry lock bits. Inducing a fatal error destroys the KeyVault contents rather than preserving them.

evidence.key_observation: The signal connected to the kv module's flush port is debug_lock_or_scan_mode_switch, driven at src/integration/rtl/caliptra_top.sv:770 by four producer terms of which one is cptra_error_fatal, the top-level fatal output (kv_flush_signal_producer_terms=4, kv_flush_signal_fatal_error_terms=1, contrast_signal_fatal_error_terms=0). Measured on the DUT: unlocked entry 3 provisioned at 0xc0de0001 and readable; entry 4 locked for use, read suppressed to 0x00000000 with rd_error=1; entry 6 locked for writes, KEY_CTRL=0x00000201, still readable at 0xc0de0004 since lock_wr does not gate reads. After one flush pulse, entry 3 reads 0xaaaaaaaa, entry 4 no longer returns its key material, and entry 6 reads 0xaaaaaaaa with its lock_wr still set, so the flush wrote through a set lock. A simultaneous two-client write to entry 5 destroyed it (0xc0de0003 to 0x00000000) with neither racing value landing. checks_run=13 checks_failed=0. Probe: cptra_in_debug_scan_mode alone, with no CLEAR_SECRETS poke, flushed nothing (probe_entry_flushed_by_debug_scan_mode_alone=0). Fatal register: fatal_register_error_fields=4, fatal_register_keyvault_fields=0, fatal_register_write_enable_sites=4, fatal_register_keyvault_write_enables=0, soc_ifc_keyvault_error_ports=0. Observability: keyvault_error_status_encodings=2, engine_register_blocks_with_keyvault_error_status=4, keyvault_client_error_assignment_sites=4, keyvault_interrupt_tieoff_sites=2. Specifications: spec_fatal_error_recovery_requirements=1, spec_hardware_keyvault_clear_conditions=2, spec_statements_requiring_keyvault_errors_reported_fatal=0. proposition_a_conclusion=a_fatal_error_already_reaches_the_keyvault_flush; proposition_b_conclusion=no_in_tree_requirement_and_keyvault_errors_are_reported_per_engine.
evidence.flush_mechanism_present: flush_keyvault (src/keyvault/rtl/kv.sv:122-123) forces a write of debug_value (src/keyvault/rtl/kv.sv:125) into every dword of every entry through the write mux at src/keyvault/rtl/kv.sv:210-217, and src/keyvault/rtl/kv.sv:211 lets the switch input stand in for the ~lock_wr_q & ~lock_use_q qualifier so locked entries are flushed too. Separately, kv_multi_write_err (src/keyvault/rtl/kv.sv:147) routes into key_entry_clear for every entry at src/keyvault/rtl/kv.sv:159, which is the KeyVault's own internal error response.

non_findings: The KeyVault flush not firing on a fatal error: withdrawn on the facts. The signal connected to the module's flush port carries cptra_error_fatal as one of four producer terms at src/integration/rtl/caliptra_top.sv:770. The claim came from reading src/keyvault/rtl/kv.sv:122-123 in isolation, where the input is named after only two of the four conditions it actually delivers.

No KeyVault field in CPTRA_HW_ERROR_FATAL: confirmed as a fact and withdrawn as a defect, as the plan pre-committed. No in-tree statement requires the report, and KeyVault failures are reported per engine through the KV status ERROR field in four engine register blocks, which is strictly more information than a global bit. The only in-tree fatal error requirement, docs/CaliptraIntegrationSpecification.md:949, constrains recovery rather than classification.

A KeyVault error input existing on soc_ifc_top but going unused: checked and absent. soc_ifc_top's only KeyVault ports are kv_read and kv_rd_resp, neither an error input (soc_ifc_keyvault_error_ports=0). Had such a port existed and been left unconnected, that would have been a reportable routing gap independent of the specification question.

OPEN QUESTION, reported on its own terms and deliberately not merged into proposition B: kv_error_intr and kv_notif_intr are assigned 1'b0 with a TODO comment at src/integration/rtl/caliptra_top.sv:473-474, while the VeeR interrupt vectors VEER_INTR_VEC_KV_ERROR and VEER_INTR_VEC_KV_NOTIF are wired to consume them at src/integration/rtl/caliptra_top.sv:485-486 (keyvault_interrupt_tieoff_sites=2). So the KeyVault's dedicated interrupt vectors are allocated but carry nothing. This is a different observability path from the SoC-facing fatal register, and letting it stand in as evidence for proposition B would overstate that claim: firmware still learns of a KeyVault access failure synchronously through the initiating engine's KV status ERROR field, which is the path the design actually uses. Whether an unused-but-allocated interrupt vector is a defect depends on whether any in-tree statement promises an interrupt-driven KeyVault error report; no such statement was found. What would settle it is a specification statement on KeyVault interrupt behavior, or firmware in the tree that waits on those vectors.

Recorded without a verdict: cptra_in_debug_scan_mode asserted on its own, with no software poke of CLEAR_SECRETS.wr_debug_values, flushes nothing (probe_entry_flushed_by_debug_scan_mode_alone=0). This is what src/keyvault/rtl/kv.sv:123 implements, since that term is qualified by the software-written field, which resets to zero. Whether hardware ought to flush on entering debug or scan mode without a software poke is a separate question from this case's two propositions. The relevant in-tree statements, docs/CaliptraIntegrationSpecification.md:249-250, describe clearing on the transition into debug mode and on the transition into scan mode, and both transitions are covered by the debug_lock_switch and scan_mode_switch terms of the connected flush signal, which the CONTROL groups show working. The steady-state mode signal is a different condition from the transition.

The simultaneous two-client write measurement (CONTROL_E) is reported as the KeyVault's own internal error response and not as a finding. Two write clients targeting one entry in the same cycle destroyed the entry's contents rather than letting either write land, which is what src/keyvault/rtl/kv.sv:147 and :159 specify. Notably neither client's kv_wr_resp.error was raised in that cycle; the destruction is the response. That observation is recorded here because it bears on how a KeyVault internal error is surfaced, but it is not part of either proposition and was not asserted as a defect.
conclusion: False alarm on both propositions. Proposition A is wrong on the facts: the kv module's flush input is named after a debug or scan mode switch, but the signal connected to it at src/integration/rtl/caliptra_top.sv:1208 is driven by four terms including cptra_error_fatal, so a fatal error does destroy KeyVault secrets. The claim came from reading the module-internal expression without tracing the connected signal, and the term detector's contrast check confirms the positive reading discriminates. That the flush matters was measured rather than assumed: it overwrites an unlocked entry with the debug value and writes that same value through a set write lock, so it is a containment mechanism the lock bits cannot stop. Proposition B is factually correct but not a defect: CPTRA_HW_ERROR_FATAL carries exactly four enumerated error conditions and no KeyVault term, but no in-tree statement requires one, and KeyVault read and write failures are reported to software per engine through the KV status ERROR field in four engine register blocks, attributable to the engine that suffered them. Two items are left explicitly open rather than folded into the verdict: the tied-off kv_error_intr and kv_notif_intr vectors, which are a distinct observability path from the fatal register, and the fact that the steady-state debug or scan mode signal flushes nothing without a software poke, where the specification speaks about the transitions that the connected signal does cover.
